images.caption: The 'Dinghuis' in Maastricht, The Netherlands. The building has been used for political and juridical purposes, and later used to be a theater. Currently, the bottom floor contains the Tourist Information Office. The name is derived from the Dutch word 'geding', which means 'lawsuit' and stems from the original use as a courtroom. So not to be confused with the Dutch word 'ding', which means 'thing', a common misconception.

images.caption: Maastricht, the Netherlands. View towards the South of Charles Eyckpark and Maaspuntweg along the Meuse river in the Céramique neighbourhood. The park was created in 1999-2000 after a design by Swedish landscape architect Gunnar Martinson and is named after the dutch painter and sculptor Charles Eyck. To the left: the Stoa building (designed by Luigi Snozzi). Far end of the road: Bonnefantenmuseum (designed by Aldo Rossi). Far right: Kennedy Bridge.

images.caption: Maastricht, the Netherlands. View towards the East of Plein 1992, the main square of the Céramique neighbourhood on the East bank of the river Meuse, named after the Treaty of Maastricht (1992). The square was designed in the late 1990s by Dutch architect Jo Coenen, as well as several buildings around it, including the Centre Céramique library on the right. To the left: part of La Résidence by Swiss architect Aurelio Galfetti and French architect Yann Keromnes. At the far end: a fragment of La Fortezza by Mario Botta.
